question.text: If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x = -2$ and $f(-2) = 2,$ then what is the value of \[ \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to \left(-2\right)} \left(\left(f(x)\right)^2+4\right)} \, ? \]
question.explanation:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=-2.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that $\lim\limits_{x\to (-2)} f(x)$ exists and \[ \lim_{x\to \left(-2\right)} f(x)=f(-2)=2. \]

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \displaystyle{\lim_{x\to \left(-2\right)} \left(\left(f(x)\right)^2+4\right)} & = \left( 2^2 + 4\right) = 8. \end{align*}

example.title: Applying the Definition of Continuity to Evaluate a Limit

question.text: For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=1?$ \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} x, & x \leq 1 \\ -x, & x > 1 \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=1.$

  • $f(1) = 1,$ so $f(1)$ exists. ${\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide: \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) &= \lim_\limits{x \to 1^-} (x) \\[5pt] &= 1, \\[10pt] \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+} f(x) &= \lim_\limits{x \to 1^+} (-x) \\[5pt] &= -(1)\\[5pt] &= -1. \end{align*} So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. $\, \, {\color{red}\times}$ $\\ \\[1ex]$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x = 1$ because $\lim_\limits{x\to 1^-} f(x) \neq \lim_\limits{x\to 1^+} f(x).$

example.title: Identifying the Reason for a Discontinuity

question.text: For what reason does the function $f(x)$ below have a discontinuity at $x = -1?$ \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} x^3+x, & x < -1 \\[3pt] x^2+1, & x \geq -1 \end{cases} \]
question.explanation:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

  • $f(-1) = (-1)^2 + 1 = 2,$ so $f(-1)$ exists. ${\color{green}\checkmark}$

  • We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide: \begin{align*} \lim_\limits{x\to (-1)^-} f(x) &= \lim_\limits{x \to (-1)^-} (x^3 + x)\\[5pt] &= (-1)^3 + (-1) \\[5pt] &= -2, \\[10pt] \lim_\limits{x\to (-1)^+} f(x) &= \lim_\limits{x \to (-1)^+} (x^2 + 1) \\[5pt] &= (-1)^2 + 1\\[5pt] &= 2. \end{align*} So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. $\, \, {\color{red}\times}$ $\\ \\[1ex]$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x = -1$ because $\lim_\limits{x\to (-1)^-} f(x) \neq \lim_\limits{x\to (-1)^+} f(x).$
